title: The project management office (PMO)
blurb: What a PMO provides, the difference between temporary and permanent PMOs, and why it supports rather than replaces the PM and sponsor.
question: A housing association runs twelve projects. Its PMO notices that three are reporting delays and their risk data is inconsistent. What should the PMO do, and what should it leave to the project managers and sponsors?

teach.body: APM describes a project management office (PMO) as an organisational structure that provides support to projects. It supplies standards, methods, templates and tools; gathers reporting and information; supports governance and gives assurance; helps with planning, scheduling and resources; and builds skills through training and expertise. In plain English: the PMO is the support hub that helps projects run well and consistently, but it does not run them itself.

teach.h: A memory aid: PMOs help projects become STARS
teach.caption: STARS is our memory aid, not an APM term. The exam lists these functions in its own words.

teach.body: A PMO helps the people who hold the real roles; it does not take those roles over. The project manager still manages the project day to day. The sponsor is still accountable and still owns the business case. The governance board still makes the decisions. The PMO's assurance role is an independent check that agreed processes and standards are followed, and its reports help the decision-makers decide well.

steps.label: PMO collates
steps.sub: Checks data is complete and consistent

teach.body: Harbourside Homes has a permanent PMO supporting twelve projects. It gives every project manager the same risk register template, trains new project managers and collates monthly reports for the executive board. A health check (an assurance review) finds one refurbishment project three weeks behind. The PMO reports this to the board. The project's manager prepares the recovery plan, and the sponsor decides whether to approve it.

rows.label: Providing a standard risk register template
Managing one project day to day

teach.text: Exam distractors give the PMO powers it does not have: 'owns the project budget', 'manages each project's scope', 'approves gate decisions', 'replaces the project manager'. The PMO SUPPORTS: standards, reporting, assurance, planning support and training. Decisions and accountability stay with the PM, the sponsor and the board.

items: PMO: an organisational structure that provides support to projects.
Functions: standards, methods, templates and tools; reporting; governance support and assurance; planning, scheduling and resource support; training and expertise.
Temporary PMOs serve one project or programme; permanent PMOs serve the organisation or portfolio.
The PMO supports; it does not replace the project manager, the sponsor or the board.

summary: You can now define a PMO, list the support it provides, tell a temporary PMO from a permanent one, and explain why the PMO supports the project manager, sponsor and board without taking over their responsibilities.

A.q: Which best describes a project management office (PMO)?
options: The board that approves each gate
The team that builds the outputs
A.why: A PMO is an organisational structure that provides support to projects.

whyNot.0: Gate approval is a governance board function.
whyNot.1: The project team builds the outputs.
whyNot.3: The sponsor is accountable for benefits.

A.q: Which of the following is a typical function of a PMO?
options: Accepting outputs on behalf of users
Chairing every project's steering group meeting
A.why: Providing standards, methods, templates and tools is a core PMO function.

whyNot.1: The sponsor owns the business case.
whyNot.2: End users (and, on iterative work, the product owner) accept outputs.
whyNot.3: The sponsor usually chairs the steering group.

A.q: A PMO set up only for the life of one major programme is best described as:
A.why: A PMO set up for one project or programme, closing when that work ends, is a temporary PMO.

whyNot.0: A permanent PMO serves the organisation or portfolio on an ongoing basis.
whyNot.2: A steering group is a governance board that makes decisions, not a support office.
whyNot.3: A portfolio board directs a whole portfolio; it is not a support office.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of a PMO?
options: Making go or no-go decisions at gates
B.why: Gate decisions are taken by the sponsor or governance board. The PMO may support the review but does not decide.

whyNot.0: Governance support and assurance is a PMO function.
whyNot.1: Reporting and information is a PMO function.
whyNot.2: Training and expertise is a PMO function.

B.q: A PMO acting as a centre of excellence mainly provides:
B.why: As a centre of excellence the PMO builds capability through training, guidance and expertise.

whyNot.1: Funding and approvals come from the sponsor and governance.
whyNot.2: Backlog prioritisation is the product owner's job.
whyNot.3: Day-to-day delivery is managed by the project manager.

B.q: A PMO checks that a project is following the agreed processes and reports the result to the board. Which PMO function is this?
B.why: Checking that processes and standards are followed, and reporting to governance, is assurance.

whyNot.0: Scheduling support helps plan when work and resources are used.
whyNot.1: Backlog refinement is done by the product owner and team on iterative work.
whyNot.3: Benefits are owned by the sponsor, not the PMO.

C.q: A PMO health check finds a project is three weeks behind its baseline. Who is responsible for producing the recovery plan?
C.why: The PMO supports and reports, but the project manager manages the project and produces the recovery plan for the sponsor to consider.

whyNot.0: The PMO does not take over a project's management, even when it finds problems.
whyNot.1: End users use the outputs; they do not plan the recovery.
whyNot.2: The product owner prioritises the backlog; the overall recovery plan is the PM's.

C.q:
Which TWO of the following are typical PMO functions?
1) Planning and scheduling support
2) Owning the business case
3) Reporting and information
4) Accepting outputs for users
C.why: Planning and scheduling support (1) and reporting and information (3) are PMO functions.

whyNot.0: Owning the business case (2) belongs to the sponsor.
whyNot.2: Neither 2 nor 4 is a PMO function.
whyNot.3: Accepting outputs (4) is done by end users or the product owner.

C.q: Why might an organisation set up a permanent PMO rather than a temporary one?
options: To deliver one project's outputs fast
To replace the sponsor on each project
To act as the end user of the outputs
C.why: A permanent PMO works at organisation or portfolio level, bringing consistent standards, reporting and support across all projects.

whyNot.1: Supporting a single piece of work is what a temporary PMO is for.
whyNot.2: A PMO never replaces the sponsor.
whyNot.3: End users are the people who use the outputs, not a PMO.

reteach.title: The PMO is the festival's site office
reteach.question: At a big music festival, each stage has its own stage manager. There is also a site office. What does the site office do, and what does it not do?

blocks.body: The site office hands every stage manager the same checklists and radio procedures, runs the safety briefing, collects updates from every stage and gives the festival director one clear picture. It checks stages are following the safety rules. But it doesn't run any stage: if a band is late, the stage manager sorts it, and if the festival must be stopped, the director decides.

blocks.text: If an option says the PMO decides, owns or manages a project, it is almost certainly wrong. If it says the PMO provides, supports, collates or assures, it fits.

explain.body: A PMO is an organisational structure that provides support to projects. It exists to help projects succeed and to make project management consistent.

test.q: Complete the statement: a PMO is an organisational structure that…
options: owns the benefits from its projects
uses the outputs of its projects
test.why: A PMO is an organisational structure that provides support to projects.

whyNot.0: Strategy is set by the organisation's senior leadership.

explain.body: Standards, methods, templates and tools; reporting and information; governance support and assurance; planning, scheduling and resource support; training and expertise.

items.label: families of PMO support to remember

test.q: A new project manager asks where to find the organisation's standard progress report format. Who is best placed to provide it?
test.why: Standards, methods and templates are provided by the PMO.

whyNot.0: The sponsor receives reports but does not maintain organisational templates.
whyNot.1: End users use the outputs; they don't hold project templates.
whyNot.2: A supplier would not hold the client organisation's standard formats.

explain.body: A temporary PMO is set up for one project or programme and closes when it ends. A permanent PMO works at organisation or portfolio level and keeps going.

test.q: A permanent PMO usually operates at which level?
test.why: A permanent PMO supports the organisation or its portfolio on an ongoing basis.

whyNot.1: A work package is far too small a unit for a PMO to be built around.
whyNot.2: Time boxes are managed by iterative teams, not by a permanent PMO.
whyNot.3: Supplier contracts are managed through procurement.

explain.body: The PMO helps the project manager, sponsor and board do their jobs. It does not take over management, accountability or decisions, even when a project struggles.

test.q: A project starts to struggle. What is the PMO's proper response?
options: Take over and run the project itself
Support and report, not take over
Cancel the project without referring up
test.why: The PMO supports the project and reports to governance; management stays with the PM and decisions with the sponsor or board.

whyNot.0: The PMO does not replace the project manager.
whyNot.2: The PMO does not replace the sponsor.
whyNot.3: Cancelling a project is a governance decision, not a PMO one.
